utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Sorry about the long delay. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Bronagh McKenna, Dan Saxon, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Novak Lukic and Boris Zorko for the Defence of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Once again, the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, in Judge David's absence. Do you want to call the witness, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means, Your Honour. While we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, given that we have a late start are we going to have a break in an hour and 15 minutes as usual? I should like to know to organise my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think let's go for an hour and 15 minutes as usual, and then we'll try to adjust as we go along. I tried to do it now mentally but I couldn't work it out. I need paper, so we'll work it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As you please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrbic -- I beg your pardon. Put on your headphones. Good morning, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope you had a restful night. We're sorry that we started late. We had technical problems with these gadgets, the technological gadgets that we have here, and I hope you were not bored waiting for us to get started since 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have understanding for my colleagues. I do know something about technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Just to remind you, Mr. Skrbic, that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us resume where we stopped yesterday, and that's, let me remind you, the point where you were appointed assistant commander in the 2nd Krajina Corps for moral, religious affairs, which is roughly between end of 1993 and the summer of 1994. Let us remind ourselves of that time. Can you briefly describe for Their Honours what the tasks and duties were of your department and specifically of you as the assistant commander for that particular field.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the very name of the department suggests, the tasks were - and I will briefly describe them - to follow and monitor the situation with regard to the morale of the 2nd Krajina Corps within the VRS and to file a periodical, that's to say monthly, reports to the VRS superior levels and the commander himself in fact. This is an important area in every army. We would inform the general public through the mass media about the activities in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps. We also published a paper of ours which was called the "Krajina Fighter," Krajiski Borac. And as far as the legal affairs are concerned, our role was that of an administrative organ, although in my department I had a professional lawyer who had been a judge before the war in Bosanski Petrovac. Since he was mobilised, he was a member of my department. Our prominent role was to tour the brigades and talk to troops about the problems they had, to furnish them with cigarettes if we had any, to inform them of the situation in other units and the corps as a whole if we had any such information. That would briefly sum up the role that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In professional terms, who was your superior or subordinate along the professional chain of command in the VRS and what sort of relationship existed between you and the Main Staff, if any, in the field of morale and religious affairs and information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the issue of morale, I could not address the Main Staff on any issues if I did not have the approval of the commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps. However, in professional terms - and this is what you asked me about in your question - I co-operated for the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you toured the defence lines and you talked to troops. What problems were there with regard to the morale in the VRS at the time you were a member of the 2nd Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the difficulties that were experienced by those on the front lines had their bearing on the morale, be it negative or positive. The troops put a number of questions to us, many of whom we could not answer specifically. For that reason, we would periodically write reports and send them to brigade commanders. The idea behind this was to brief them on all these issues; although, we knew up front that some of these problems could not be resolved easily since the front lines were spread out and we knew that many of the troops would never receive the information that we sent down to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Republika Srpska did there exist the system of military judiciary, in other words, a system of military prosecutor's offices and military courts?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did there exist, and if so at which level, military disciplinary courts in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of corps there existed military disciplinary courts, at the level of all corps save for the 2nd Krajina Corps. In that respect we had to rely on the military disciplinary court of the 1st Krajina Corps. The 1st Krajina Corps was headquartered in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the members of the command, including the command, meet; did they have regular meetings; and if so, how frequently would they meet during your time there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two types of meeting at the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps. One set of meetings would normally take place every morning in the operations centre of the 2nd Krajina Corps. It would be a briefing where we would receive all the intelligence that had been gathered, and we would be issued with direct tasks. The second sort of meetings were meetings of the commanders of all the units of the 2nd Krajina Corps, where issues would be discussed as per the various fields and they could be summed up as follows: Operational field, morale, logistics issues --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And another one the interpreter didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the third type of professional line -- field that was mentioned. Can the witness please repeat that. She caught operation field, morale, logistic issues --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Personnel I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personnel issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your time in the 2nd Krajina Corps and when participating in these meetings, what sort of information did you have on how the logistics sector functioned in the 2nd Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the operational and combat issues, logistics posed the gravest of problems. That's because the 2nd Krajina Corps did not have a proper logistics support; rather, through a set of coincidences the brigades of the 2nd Krajina Corps had to rely on municipal bodies for logistics. There were also donors in that regard, and occasionally we would be given the logistics support from the Croatian army. The 2nd Krajina Corps otherwise relied on the 14th Logistics Base, which was headquartered in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested specifically in the following. You said that you would occasionally be assisted by the Croatian army as well. Can you clarify this? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian army provided resources for the HVO, and I think it was in the area of Zepce. That's opposite the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps. They particularly provided fuel and we were in shortage of that. The agreement was that once they would be transporting fuel and transiting the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps, they should leave behind a certain amount of fuel. But this arrangement was in place for as long as there existed the conflict with the Army of -- the Muslim army, the BH army. Afterwards, the deal was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've explained this quite clearly for Their Honours and I don't want to lead you in any way. Can you tell us what happened if there were a certain number of tanker trucks involved?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no need for you to lead me on anything. I told you during proofing that if we agree that three tanker trucks would be on their way with fuel, two of them would proceed on and one would be left behind in our territory, stay with us. That was the deal. Let me add that we did not in any way seize it from them. It was their offer in exchange for passage across the territory of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up document P1011.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will first look at page 1 and then at the last page. I'm primarily interested in the form of the document, not the contents. On page 1 it is written "Sector For Morale and Religious Affairs." And then the date is the 27th of May, 1993, daily report number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the last page of the document, please. And if we could enlarge the bottom part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It states: "Information service, to be delivered to the Main Staff of the VRS, PKM1, KK, 2 KK, IBK, SRK, DK, HK, V, and PVL, and then it's stated GS/VJ (administration for information) Ministry of Defence of the FRY." This is a document dating back to the period when you were still a member of the Army of Yugoslavia in the administration for information of the General Staff. Can I first ask you whose document this is because the heading isn't that specific.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you've explained what the heading of the document was, which said that it was a document from the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. You then explained who the document was addressed to, but you referred to abbreviations only. If need be, Your Honours, I can give you the full titles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No need for that. I'll ask you specifically about one of these acronyms, but my first question is this. While you were on the administration for information of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, did you have occasion to see documents such as this one, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at a copy of a document whose authenticity is beyond doubt, but a document such as this one is not something I had occasion to see while I was in the administration for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If such documents had been sent to the administration for information, would they have been sent to the chief of the administration, to you personally, or specifically tell us was it your duty to be acquainted with all the documents that were received by the administration?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents that were sent to the administration would end up on the desk of the chief of the administration, who would in turn decide on a need-to-know basis who it was who had to be acquainted with it. The contents of this document are such that the chief of the administration could have understood the document to have been sent to him for his information. In other words, he didn't have to forward it to anyone. He could have only asked the secretary to file it in the archives. However, where documents contained information that was important in his view, he would inform members of the administration thereof at meetings that were held specifically for briefing. He would not, in that case, mention the source of that particular information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the start of 1994 you held the position of the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs in the 2nd Krajina Corps. We were able to see that the document back then in May of 1995 was also sent to the KK. What does this abbreviation stand for -- that it was sent to the 2nd KK, what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The acronym 2 KK stands for the 2nd Krajina Corps, but this isn't the sort of document that I was able to see in the 2nd Krajina Corps nor did the -- such documents come there later on. The document states or purports to be a daily report. If you go back to the start of the document, you'll see that it is a daily report. And with your leave, I can tell you what sort of information we received in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to make sure that the record is clear, the English transcript, line 10, page 9, in the question from Mr. Lukic describes the document as being from May of 1995. That may be an error because both versions appear to say "May 1993." I just wanted to keep the record clear. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we say it's from May 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Must have been a mistake, either I made a mistake or a typo, but the witness spoke about May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Lukic. I -- you said to the witness a little earlier that at the time of the issue of this document he was in the administration of the VJ in the information service, and you asked him whether he had occasion to receive it while he was there, and he says he never saw it. Now you're asking him about the KK, which is the Krajina Corps, and asking him whether he saw it while he was there. Now, in 1993 he was in the administration of the VJ. There's no way he could see this document in the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the document in May 1995 was sent to the administration and the 2nd Krajina Corps, what I wanted to know is whether the witness, once he went to the Krajina Corps, whether he saw such documents. So after 1994 whether such reports were sent to the Krajina Corps. That was the second level of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you then saying you don't take Mr. Saxon's correction of line 10 of page 9 because you really did mean 1995? That now in 1995 he was now in the 2nd Krajina Corps -- and therefore what are you saying? Anyway, what you are saying is sequentially when he was in the administration he didn't -- did he see it; and when he finally came to the Krajina Corps, did he also see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intention was to see whether there was a continuity of these reports of the Prosecution in the entire period mentioned in the indictment. The OTP offered evidence for 1993. I was interested in exploring whether such documents existed in 1994 because this witness was at the position, he held the position where he was supposed to receive such reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, while you were in the 2nd Krajina Corps at the position of the assistant for morale, but -- so it was end of 1993 until the summer of 1994, what kind of information did you receive from the Main Staff, from the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs, and how often did you receive such information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, we would receive information on a monthly basis. The content of that information concerned the state of morale in the Army of Republika Srpska. The information was compiled on the basis of analysis and sublimation of the data which the sector had received from all corps, independent units, and air force and anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information coming from the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska could not be sent to the units without prior knowledge of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in proofing I showed to this witness this particular document, P1011, and all other documents up to P1066. I have informed Mr. Saxon about it. These are daily reports of the same kind, day by day. So as not to show all of these individual documents to the witness, I just wanted to ask the witness to confirm that I have showed these documents to him and to confirm that what he has said just now pertains to all other five documents. I apologise, it should be P1016. These are daily reports of the type that you see on the screen, just on sequential days. The last report is dated 18th of June, 1993. So for that brief period of time we have five documents. If I were to put a general question to the witness and ask him whether this pertains to all other five documents I have showed him during proofing, then would you approve that that would be an appropriate way to proceed without showing each individual document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're doing something that is never done, Mr. Lukic. Maybe -- Mr. Saxon, do you have any comment to make on what he is saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think it would be more helpful if very briefly we could hear a comment on the document because this may affect what I do with my cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On this series of five or six documents that Mr. Lukic has just -- has just mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's what he wants to do, he wants to get a comment from him on a generalised basis that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- I think what he was asking if he were to be shown the other five would these comments be the same as his comments were on this one. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear -- before I take a final position, I'd like to hear the question, but -- if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, in proofing I showed you six documents similar to the one you see on the screen. One is dated 28th of May, 1993; and then there is another one on the same date indicating that it was the second daily report for that day; and then we have another document on the 29th of May, 1993, daily report number 1; and then 29th of May of 1993, daily report number 2; and then finally 18th of August, 1993, or perhaps 18th of June, again the same kind of document. Do you remember me showing you these documents such as this one in proofing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You showed all of these documents to me. Their contents are very similar and my comment would be completely identical to the one I gave in relation to the first document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the transcript interprets your question as saying "and then finally 18th of August, 1993, or perhaps 18th of June ..." Now, is it August or is it June? Because it doesn't say "or rather," it says "or perhaps."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Let us be as specific as possible concerning this document. Let us put this document only on the screen, it's P1016 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it the 18th of August or is it the 18th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it well. It's not very legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Truly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Put it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the B/C/S heading please be enlarged. It looks more like an 8, 08, to me, Your Honours, although I'm not fully certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, it's looks like the English translation gave it August, and then of course there's a question mark before the month. It is what it says. I don't know what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going through the text to see whether there would be some indication there, but I really can't find my way in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Lukic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, let us now go to your new appointment. Please tell us, when did you transfer to the Main Staff, pursuant to whose decision, and to what position were you appointed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps, General Boris, received a cable from the Main Staff of the VRS, indicating that Colonel Petar Skrbic was to report to the Main Staff of the VRS on an urgent basis in a day or two. I was informed about this by the corps commander. He told me that he knew nothing about it, but I had to pack my things and report to the Main Staff of the VRS. Therefore, based on that cable I went to the Main Staff of the VRS I think on the 27th of July. Should I repeat something?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no. Thank you. Could we now see on the screens part of your personnel file, 1D12-0319 is the English version. And could we also call -- all right. Here it is. I'm being told that the draft English translation is linked with this number so that the Judges can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just wondering, to make it easier to follow along, is this document -- does this particular document have a Defence 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This document is part of the personnel file of Mr. Skrbic. The B/C/S has a -- is marked as P1688, but this was not admitted into evidence, this particular portion, even though it constitutes a part of the personnel file. I think that we have marked it as such. 65 ter of the OTP 07837. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, what do we see now on our screens? What document is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we scroll down, please, to see who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I see on the screen is a document which is a copy of the presidential decree of the president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, which indicates that Colonel Skrbic was appointed to the establishment position in the sector for organisational, mobilisation, and personnel affairs. Given that this is an establishment position that requires a rank of a general, then it is only the president of the republic who is authorised to appoint persons to this position, which in this case was done by the rules, by the president of the republic. Could we now scroll up so I can tell you about something else that I saw on the document. You see that this document was handed in to me personally, and this signature or initials are my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean the ones in the upper right corner, handwritten initials?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It is in -- you can see in the Cyrillic script it says "to the appointee," and then underneath you see my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on which regulations did the president of VRS -- or rather, based on whose regulations did the president of the VRS issue this presidential decree?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the preamble of this presidential decree there is a specific reference as to the regulations on the basis of which this presidential decree was issued. It says here "pursuant to the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska," Article 11 and so on, and then there's an indication of the "Official Gazette" in which this law was published. So this was done on the basis of the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was your predecessor in that position, in the position to which you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before me this position was held by General Mico Grubor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see another document on the screens, a document coming from the same source which is a personnel file of Colonel Skrbic which was admitted into evidence as P1688. Could we now see 1D12-0317.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we take this one off, Mr. Lukic, what was the number of this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, this one. This --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous, yes, I would like to tender it into evidence, but since we only have draft translation perhaps we should MFI it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but what was the 65 ter number of this one, this one that appoints the witness to the Republic of Srpska General Staff, sector for organisational, mobilisation --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, please. Let me check something with my case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm checking this with my case manager to make it easier for everybody. I think that in addition to the fact that this document was on the OTP 65 ter list, we also had the personnel file on our OTP list with a different number. So I will now give you the Defence 65 ter number, but I will need only certain pages from this personnel file. Give us just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On our 65 ter list it's under a wrong number. It's not a four-digit number, but it can be found under number 285. So this is why I will propose that it now be assigned the following 65 ter number: 03330D, and I seek to tender it into evidence and MFI it until the final translation comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 03330D, triple zero?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you are tendering it into evidence? You're saying you're tendering it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The document is admitted into evidence, marked for identification, may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit Number D327, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call 1D12-0317, please. Again, this is a document that comes from the personnel file and it can be found under the same number, and since I will ask that it be tendered into evidence I will now assign the following number to it, 03331D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you're taking a break and looking at the documents, can I tell you about the times now, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Instead of going to 11.25, can we go to 11.40?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't know how focused the witness will be. It's not a problem with me if we sit for a bit longer. I don't think we have the right document on our screen. I will have to call up a different number. 1D12-0321. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, what is this document about, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we see the signature block.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a copy of what is indubitably an authentic document because I recognise my signature. This is a record on the transfer of duty. General Mico Grubor handed his duty over to me, Petar Skrbic, pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was this transfer of duty like, can you describe it in a few words?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transfer of duty took place on the 14th of August, I believe, in the presence of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. There's a procedure in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will not be going into that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, no need for that. The commander congratulated me on the position and wished Mico Grubor who retired good health. He told me that there were impending tasks ahead of me and wished me good luck.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you comment on this sentence: "In the course of the transfer of duty," and this is paragraph 2, "the recipient was acquainted with work-plans and most important legal and other documents governing the work of organisational, mobilisation ..." it's a bit odd this formulation, "organisational, mobilisation, and personnel organs."

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me help with that. This is called the sector for organisational, mobilisation, and personnel-related affairs. My predecessor, General Grubor, handed over to me all the documents related to the work of the sector; otherwise, my signature certifying that I received my duties would have been pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you also comment on the last paragraph: "The person who handed over his duty introduced his successor with the methodology of work in the Main Staff of the VRS and the manner of work related to the workings of this sector ..." What was it that Mr. Grubor told you on the occasion? What was it that he briefed you on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 27th of July, 1994, and the 14th of August, the transfer of duty had to be fully carried out. He informed me in that period what had been done by that point and what was left still for me to do in the future. He also acquainted me with the work methodology and with the relationship between that sector and the commander of the Main Staff and the way in which documentation had to be prepared for the meeting of commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours. We have a draft translation here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification. Can Mr. Lukic confirm that this document, like the last one, originates from what is Prosecution P1688; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's part and parcel of the personnel file.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a question. I'm not objecting to the admission of the document. Perhaps this is a question for the Court Officer. I'm just wondering whether it might be a more clear practice for the record to add these additional documents to the existing exhibit, the existing -- which presently has the number P1688 rather than giving it a Defence exhibit number. But I am in the Court's hands on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Court is in the hands of the parties, actually, on that. You tell us what you want to do. Mr. Court -- Mr. Registrar, you might perhaps want to guide us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if these documents have not been tendered or admitted in evidence by the OTP or admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber, then there is no need for them to be admitted under the same exhibit number. It is basically up to the parties to decide how to proceed. The Registry will support one or the other way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand, Mr. Registrar's point. He says: "If these documents have not been tendered or admitted in evidence by the OTP or admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber, then there is no need for them to be admitted under the same ..." Okay. So they can be given a new number. Okay. Give them a new number, take them under your testimony. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm just thinking for the record down the road, Your Honour, wouldn't it be simpler to have a single exhibit containing all the documents, the subdocuments, that each party wants as part of that exhibit, particularly when we're talking about complex and voluminous exhibits or files such as a personnel file ? In the case of Mr. Skrbic, his personnel file contains many, many pages. I don't know what Mr. Lukic's position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, I am fully in agreement with Mr. Saxon on this score. The Prosecution has had admitted a part of the personnel file of Mr. Skrbic as their exhibit. This relates to his status mostly. When at one point we will be analysing the case file and you will be examining it too, it would be useful to have the personnel file in one exhibit rather than have to put the various pieces together. We will have more of such situations as this one. We will have portions of personnel files of certain individuals presented here, other portions of which were already admitted previously as Prosecution exhibits. So perhaps in this way we would make it easier for us to examine these exhibits at some point. Because you will have portions admitted as Prosecution exhibits where they will try to show that he was part of the personnel centre, then you will also have our exhibits which will be part of his same file. Maybe this will be easier for all the parties involved at some point when they go back to these exhibits. It's a suggestion of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then there -- there should be a way of alerting the Chamber which documents which form part of the same exhibit were tendered by the Prosecution and which by the Defence, because otherwise we -- I'm just thinking when we are writing the judgement, we should be able to know what is Defence evidence and what is Prosecution evidence. And if we're going to find an exhibit that is a P exhibit containing Defence documents inside without us knowing that those documents came from the Defence, we might treat them as Prosecution documents and I don't -- all I'm saying is we need a workable way. And the reason I was saying you put it in as a Defence exhibit to us because I wanted to see what is Defence evidence and what is Prosecution evidence, but at the same time I realise that if we're having voluminous exhibits it's -- doesn't serve the purpose to duplicate what's already in there. The question, however, here is in P1688 are these documents there, these documents that you are showing us on the screen, are they already there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what is -- the question now is the way you regard these documents. These are documents P1688 in terms of the B/C/S which has hundreds of pages. However, the Prosecution has only asked to admit a dozen of the pages of this document. So I suppose you would only have in English translated those portions that the Prosecution has asked to have admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As you might be aware, the Chamber is illiterate in B/C/S. So the hundreds of pages in B/C/S that are part of 1688 mean absolutely nothing to the Chamber, only the English ones would mean something. So your English ones will also mean something. The question is when they come into P1688, the Chamber must be able to identify which are tendered by the Defence and which are tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't offer you a solution on that really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then -- okay. But then I'm asking you the question: Are your English parts of P1688, the ones that you are tendering today, are they already in the Prosecution's P1688?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They didn't want to have portions of the document translated that they weren't interested in, and I understand their position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then if they are not already in P1688, I think they might as well come in as a Defence exhibit. Because P1688 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously this is something that we'll have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P1688 doesn't have them as we stand, as things stand right now, in English; it has them in B/C/S and we are not going to read the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then -- the document then, if there is no objection to it being admitted, it's been admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D328.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is this official translation or not or shall we mark it for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's a draft translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then it's marked for identification. Is there a way, even though this is a Defence exhibit, in which we can indicate its link to P1688? Is there a way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Registrar is very kindly going to make a note in the transcript to link it, this one and the previous one. Henceforth, if there are any such links, can we mention that so that he can make that link. And if you don't mention it, he won't do it because he won't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It will be helpful to all of us. Can we now call up the Defence 65 ter document 00483D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What we have on our screens is the decision on the establishment organisation, formation, command and control of the Army of Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time this document was made, Mr. Skrbic, you were not a member of the VRS; but are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the document because my predecessor handed over to -- handed it over to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you explain in a few words what this is all about, us being laymen in this field?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terms this document is an organisational order for the setting up of the Army of Republika Srpska, in view of the fact that the Army of Republika Srpska was set up on the 12th of May, 1992, pursuant to a decision of the National Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn now to the next page. I'm interested in item 4. Can we look -- see item 4, can we go either up or down because we don't see it in the B/C/S, item 4. I think it's further down in relation to this portion. No, we need the next page, the bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Item 4 reads as follows: "The command and control of operational groups on the front shall be carried out by the Main Staff of the Army of Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is immediately subordinated to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." To your knowledge, was this the way and the basis on which the army units operated throughout the war in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the sake of precision, let me say this: The formulations used in item 4 were modified to a certain extent because the Army of Republika Srpska, i.e., the Main Staff, was subordinated to the president of Republika Srpska, and that's the modification involved. Other than that, the superior/subordinate relationship has been reflected accurately. The army was subordinated to the -- to a civilian organ, to the Presidency, and at a later date to the president himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in both the B/C/S and the English. The English text starts on the previous page in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you first who the author of the document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bottom of the next page. Can we have the bottom part of the page in the B/C/S to see who the author of the document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, General.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the document was signed by the president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Radovan Karadzic. The authors of the document were members of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the members of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a very precise answer. I will read out the portion which starts at the top of the page in the B/C/S, and Their Honours can follow in English at the bottom. "In order for the commands and units of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be set up, immediately call on all the Serbian people who are members of the Yugoslav People's Army to place themselves at the disposal of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with their entire equipment and weapons, either individually or with their units." We discussed this yesterday. Were you aware of the fact that at the time there was issued a public proclamation by the authorities of Republika Srpska, calling upon JNA members outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is this something that is consistent with your memory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course this does not only relate to the territory of the FRY, it also relates to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you -- can we please have your comments on the next paragraph as well. "The commands of corps, brigades, regiments, and support units shall be formed from members of the JNA who refuse or reject the decision of the FRY Presidency to withdraw to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Equip and arm them with the equipment and weapons that those who are now members of the JNA would place at the disposal of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Yesterday, we saw a document where the president -- where the Presidency of Yugoslavia was mentioned, which has to do with this. And can we have your comments on it. It was a closed session of the Presidency. Or let me ask you this: If the Presidency of the FRY had called on members of the JNA to return to the FRY, was this an obligation on their part to do so or what were the consequences involved if they refused to comply with this decision and stayed on in the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina, later to become the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this wouldn't really be the military terminology that would be used where it is stated where they refused to comply with the decision of the Presidency. Well, it does, however, reflect accurately the situation as it existed. There were individuals who refused to comply with this decision. There were also individuals among them who were not native Bosnians, but they were serving in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were 176 of them who hailed from Macedonia, Serbia, even Croatia and who decided and said that they would stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this translation here is official?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D329. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have another document from the 65 ter list of the Defence -- just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I wanted to call a document on the screen, but I have just been told that the translation is not yet available. Perhaps it will be available tomorrow. Let me ask you, however, what is an order on specifying jurisdiction and relationship between senior officers in the Army of Republika Srpska? Do you know anything about that document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order that you're mentioning has to do with accurate regulating of jurisdictions and powers when it comes to transferring, promoting personnel, and so on. This order can only be issued by the minister of defence, and this is something that the minister did at the very beginning of the war. The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska continually complied with the decisions of and orders of the minister of defence in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Simply speaking, what does this order do? Who decides at which level about what issues? Or perhaps you could illustrate this with an example.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document specifies clearly what it is that the corps commander does, brigade commander, commander of an independent regiment, commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. And given that this is the area that I'm most familiar with, this document also clearly specifies what powers commander of the Army of Republika Srpska has when it comes to promotions and other affairs. Let me just say this, that the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska was authorised to promote officers from the rank of major until the rank of lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Saxon stands up, you keep referring to this document. What document are you referring to, Mr. Skrbic, in your answer -- the question was: "Simply speaking, what does this order do? Who decides at which level about what issues? Or perhaps you could illustrate this with an example." And your first -- your answer was: "This document specifies ..." I'm not sure what document you're referring to. You're asking -- you're being asked about the relationship and you're referring to a document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I know exactly to which this pertains, I apologise, I thought that you would know what I know. I'm referring to the document specifying the powers, the jurisdiction, which unfortunately you don't have on the screens so you don't see the actual document. And this document on powers or competencies regulates the relations and competencies from the level of brigade up until the level of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. Mr. Saxon, you had something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two matters -- two matters, Your Honour. One is -- well, first of all, the Prosecution is feeling disadvantaged at this moment because the witness is making long explanations, referring apparently to a particular document which we don't have available. Second of all, Mr. Lukic referred to document D329. I assume that is a Defence exhibit. I don't have that on the Defence's list of exhibits that they would be using with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. -- you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This must be an interpretation mistake. I said document 00072D. That's the 65 ter number. And this document is on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic -- this 00072D, when did you refer to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on our 65 ter list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but which document is this? Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the document I was going to show to the witness, but we are lacking the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you never mentioned the number of that document. You stopped short of mentioning the number. But let me tell you -- let me take you back to what Mr. Saxon is talking about. Mr. Saxon is talking about D329. That's the last exhibit which was 65 ter 00483D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you say you don't have that on the 65 ter exhibit list of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I misunderstood and I withdraw that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The other issue you had raised was?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: 72D, Your Honour. I do have a copy of the B/C/S; however, I am still a bit at sea when we're having these long explanations by General Skrbic. And perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because you don't have the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We sent this document to CLSS a long time ago, and I have to apologise to everybody, especially to the Prosecution, for not providing at least a draft translation. This is -- but since we are lacking the translation, I thought it was better to deal with this document tomorrow when we have the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's do that, deal with it tomorrow. Can you go to the next document that has translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, have you heard of the 30th Personnel Centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when did you hear of it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't pin-point the date, but I think it was in late 1994 or at around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me phrase my question in these terms. When on the 17th of December, 1993, you went to the Army of Republika Srpska, was anything mentioned to you at the time? Did you know at that time that it existed, the 30th Personnel Centre, do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P00734.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the instructions on the way in which the special personnel centres are to work and the programme of their activity dated the 8th of December, 1993. Let me phrase the question like this: When was the first time you saw the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has he ever seen the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you place that on the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a hard copy too if you want to see that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go back to the beginning, please. Your Honours, I heard about this document in 1997 when I came to the Army of Yugoslavia, and I saw it for the first time in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When handing over duties to you, did Mr. Grubor tell you anything about the existence of this document? Did he tell you that there was such a document entitled "Instructions on the Functioning of Personnel Centres"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness has just told us that he first heard about this document in 1997 and saw it for the first time in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he said that he saw it, and I wanted to ask him whether he had heard about the existence of these instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to the witness. He heard about it in 1997 for the first time. He saw it for the first time in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when you arrived to the position of the assistant commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, from that moment on and until or while you were at the Army of Republika Srpska, did you contact anybody from the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did contact them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whom did you contact?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I mention names?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Colonel Gojko Mijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To whom -- to which army did Gojko Mijic belong, he was a member of which army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Gojko Mijic was a member of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you visit the premises of the 30th Personnel Centre while still a member of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very seldom, but I did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know at that time to whom the 30th Personnel Centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia was subordinated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly knew that. If necessary, I can tell you to whom it was subordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th Personnel Centre fell within the personnel administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who at that time headed the personnel department of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the interpretation is completed. The chief of the personnel administration at that time was General Dusan Zoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this a good time for our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After the witness's answer, yes. Okay. We've got the answer. Thank you so much. We'll take a break and come back at ten past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. You can go to the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like now to turn to another topic, namely, the structure of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with the assistance of Mr. Saxon, I have this organigram of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska from June of 1995. A similar document was used in the Popovic case when the witness testified about the structure of the Main Staff. So I would suggest that a copy in English be given to the Bench and then we also have a copy in the B/C/S and we can use hard copies to go over this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While proofing the witness I realised - and Mr. Saxon can confirm this - that the witness has a problem with the names and translations of some of the titles. So I will be putting questions to the witness and then I think we can clarify this this way. Could Mr. Skrbic see a hard copy because the font is quite small.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, I will be putting questions to you so that we can clarify the names of certain parts of the Main Staff, and then this picture will be quite useful in understanding the structure of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I'm now talking about the period of time when you arrived in the summer, in August, of 1994, until the end of the war. My first question is this -- or perhaps I should just let you comment on the organigram, to tell us who comprised the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I can't see when interpretation ends, may I begin now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska is indicated correctly. Chief of the sector for operative and staff affairs is Lieutenant-General Milovanovic, Manojlo Milovanovic. Where it says "staff" on the left side of this organigram --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Skrbic, you're saying Mr. Milovanovic is chief of the sector for operative and staff affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he's given here as chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, his exact title is as I have told you, chief of the sector for operative and staff affairs, and at the same time deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is your organigram describing the titles correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In proofing Mr. Skrbic had some observations to certain titles in B/C/S. This is a document produced by the OTP in another case. So this document in the B/C/S also reads "chief of the Main Staff." And when I asked Mr. Skrbic about this, he said that in the establishment terms of the Army of Republika Srpska General Milovanovic was as he has just told us, deputy commander and at the same time chief of the sector, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this may have been a Prosecution document in another case. You have adopted it as your exhibit and it does not speak to what your witness is saying. So -- okay, but we accept that explanation, but just note that your document doesn't speak to what your -- at least you should have amended it to suit your purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, since Mr. Skrbic has certain reservations when it comes to some titles, I will not tender this into evidence. I simply want you to follow his evidence and see the relations as indicated in organigram. As for any discrepancies between what is in the document and what Mr. Skrbic says, I won't rely on that at all. I simply want him to give evidence about the Main Staff and for you to be able to see how that looks -- how that structure looks on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can continue, Mr. Skrbic. How was the Main Staff divided, into which parts?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to give you the exact terms when it comes to the structure of the Main Staff, and this is why I made the correction I made about the chief of the Main Staff. Now I will continue. In this entire horizontal line we shouldn't have any departments. There were no departments. There were sectors. But let us now move to this area where it says "General Miletic." His name was not Radovan, his name was Radivoje, and it was administration for operations and training. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So as not to spend too much time with the document, just give us in general terms.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in general terms there should be no departments, rather, there should be sectors, sector administration for air force and anti-aircraft defence. Then we should have a sector for security and intelligence, sector for religious and morale affairs, sector for reinforcement and personnel affairs, logistical sector or sector for logistics, and administration for planning, development, and finance. These are the exact terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the head of these sectors and administrations, who was appointed to these positions in establishment terms? What was the name for the person heading a sector?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood your question, Mr. Lukic. I'm just waiting for interpretation. I'm not sure when it ends. At the head of all sectors and independent administrations within the Main Staff of the VRS, there were assistant commanders of the commander of the Main Staff of VRS who were at the same time chiefs of those sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have already heard some evidence here. There was a witness before you testifying about your sector and what it comprised. Therefore, would you please tell us now about the sector for logistics. What did it comprise? What did that sector have under it? Who headed that sector, tell us first?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sector for logistics was headed by General Djukic. That sector comprised the largest number of administrations and departments, including quartermaster service, traffic service, technical service, and medical corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say that the sector mentioned here as sector for rear services is actually the sector for logistics?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where was the headquarters of the Main Staff of VRS located, where was its seat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will now give you a very specific military terms. The main command post of the Main Staff of the VRS was in Crna Rijeka. As for the logistics command post of the Main Staff was in the Han Pijesak settlement. Crna Rijeka, where the main command post was, was some 20 kilometres away from Han Pijesak. As for the logistics or rear command post, General Djukic who headed that sector, he was located there together with all of his services as well as General Skrbic, myself, and all of my services. So all of us were located in that location. All other parts of the Main Staff were located at Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to these sectors and independent administrations, did the Main Staff of the VRS have some other additional organs of services?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. The Main Staff had independent units of the Main Staff which were the communications regiment, 67th Communications Regiment; 63rd Defence Protection Motorised Regiment; then the hospital of the Main Staff which was located at Sokolac; military medical centre of the Main Staff which was located in Banja Luka; centre for automatic processing of data, also located in Banja Luka; accounting centre, which again was in Banja Luka; and if necessary, I can also give you some additional services that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. For the needs of this trial I'm only interested in another organisational unit which is logistics bases. Do you know whether there were any logistics bases in the VRS; and if so, to whom they were subordinated in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were four logistical bases located in Banja Luka, Bileca, Bijeljina, and Sokolac. They were subordinated directly to the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS; and as for specialised affairs, they came under the chief of the sector for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a collegium or some other collective body which met within the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a collegium. I apologise if I'm rushing. I don't see the transcript, so please warn me to slow down if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the question was about the collegium. The commander of the Main Staff had two types of collegiums: The inner collegium which comprised his assistants and the expanded collegium which in addition to his assistants also included commanders of all corps and commanders of logistics bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With another witness we saw names of certain corps, and I'm sure that the Trial Chamber's already familiar with some of the names indicated here. Let me just ask you this: Who headed the independent administration for development and finances during the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact name of the administration is administration for planning, development, and finances, and it was headed by General Stevan Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already said about Gvero, that he was the head of administration for security intelligence. Can you tell us who was the head of the administration for air force and anti-aircraft defence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This administration was headed by General Jovo Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This structure of the Main Staff that you've just discussed, did it change during the war? And I mean in the period leading to the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not change.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did I hear you well that you're saying -- where is that now? Yeah. Page 42, line 14, you're saying: "You've already said about Gvero, that he was the head of administration for security intelligence." What is it you were saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said that we know already what position was held by Mr. Gvero and we know who held positions in the intelligence administration from previous testimonies. So that's why I wanted to skip that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whenever I want to speed things up, I seem to complicate them further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we should take it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We no longer need the document. It can be taken off the ELMO so that the witness can follow the transcript of his testimony. I do not wish to tender the document. I merely wanted Their Honours to follow the witness 's testimony more easily. Now that we're still on these structural issues, I will be calling up a document which is not on the 65 ter list but which I will ask that it be tendered -- that it be admitted. It was marked as dock ID 1D12-0187. And I'll call it the working or operations map of the Army of Republika Srpska. It's not contained on our 65 ter list, as I said, Your Honours. I found about this document when for the first time I talked to Mr. Skrbic a month and a half ago, when we had a proofing session after a long break, he referred to this document that was shown to him during a proofing session for his testimony in the Popovic case. I found that the document was used in open session in that case, and on the 12th of April earlier this year I sent the document to the OTP and I notified Mr. Saxon about my intention to use it. That's the first important thing that I want to mention about this document. The second point is that the document has 104 pages. It is very voluminous. In the Popovic case, only in the first seven pages of the document were translated into English. I told -- or rather, it's a list, in fact. You will see what sort of information is contained in that list, and I believe that once you do you will share my view that the entire document should be translated because the contents are of paramount importance for this trial. I wanted to see with Mr. Saxon if he agrees whether we can use the document with this witness, and if we could agree for the document to be sent to the CLSS and at a later stage in due time have it translated in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all you'll notice that I'm not standing up to address the Chamber, and I am not being disrespectful but simply a few minutes ago I began to have some difficulty with my back and it would probably take me several minutes right now to stand up and address you. So in the interests of saving time, with your leave, I will address you from this sitting position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you've taken the leave without being granted it yet, Mr. Saxon, so carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have taken the leave, Your Honour, but I felt I needed to do that. Your Honour, I would simply like to ask Mr. Lukic whether he can confirm precisely when the Defence received this document. It's my understanding that at least a portion of this document would have been provided to the Defence on the 31st of December last year as part of the Prosecution's disclosure of materials that were used with General Skrbic during his prior testimony in the case of Popovic et al., and so I'd like some more clarification, please, from Mr. Lukic on the establishment of good cause for not having placed this document on the Defence 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document, a part of which, several pages of which we received from the OTP as Mr. Saxon said in December of last year, did not constitute a significant document for us until we realised the gist of it with Mr. Skrbic, and that was only at the point when Mr. Skrbic came to The Hague and when I started my proofing session with him. This was on the 10th of April, I believe. The very next day, as soon as I realised the point of the document, its importance, and as soon as I got hold of it from the database of the file in the Popovic case, I informed Mr. Saxon about it. It took someone to show the document to me - and this was Mr. Skrbic - to indicate the information contained in the document and the significance of it. When Mr. Skrbic explained to me what sort of information can be found there, I immediately notified Mr. Saxon and told him that I wanted to use the document with the witness. The document contains names and formations of all the officers of the Army of Republika Srpska, and I mean active service officers; the date of their entry into duty into duty; and the name of the person who assigned them there. And it's not easy to comprehend the information in the document unless someone is there who can explain it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't stand up. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, briefly, the Prosecution does not believe that the Defence has established good cause for not placing this document on its Rule 65 ter list. Its Rule 65 ter list was due nearly a month after the Defence received a portion of this document. It could have evaluated the importance of the document at the end of December; the Defence did not do that and it has not -- Mr. Lukic has not provided a basis for adding it to the 65 ter list today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order for me to respond to this, you would need to have the document in front of you. This is my answer: The document does not have a title. I received several pages of the document from the Prosecution. In order for you to see what this is about, you would need to see the document on the screen and then you will decide whether I acted with due diligence or not. I acted as soon as I became aware of the contents of the document, and this was made possible only through my conversation with the person who knew something about it. And the moment I realised this, I got in touch with Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but the Defence received about half of this document from the Prosecution in March of 2007 because about half of this document was Prosecution 65 ter exhibit 5600, which the Prosecution eventually chose not to tender. So the Defence was clearly on notice of -- about the information in about half of this document several years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
